item.title: AI agents clock in at Chinese farms, factories, firms
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-28
BEIJING, Nov. 28 (Xinhua) -- At ZTE's manufacturing base in east China's Nanjing, the warehouse is in constant motion. Across more than 100,000 storage locations stacked on multiple levels, four-way shuttle vehicles dart between shelves, while lifts and stacker cranes move materials up and down. Behind this choreography is a growing digital workforce at this base consisting of over 80 AI agents. "Which box should be delivered to which point on the production line, and when, is all decided by multiple agents working together," said Zhou Jianfeng, vice president of ZTE, a telecommunications service provider. When the factory winds down for the night, a warehouse-optimization agent remains at work. Using the next day's production orders, it identifies which materials will be needed most and arranges for them to be moved closer to the production lines before the morning shift begins. The monthly distance traveled in collecting materials has dropped from more than 400,000 meters to about 160,000 meters, Zhou said, pointing to the plant's rapidly growing digital workforce. Daily token consumption in the base's supply chain operations alone has exceeded 9 billion, according to the firm. These gains at ZTE are part of a wider push by Chinese businesses to deploy AI agents across the real economy. As this technology takes on more tasks, the promise of higher productivity is accompanied by questions over whether it can deliver reliable returns and how its adoption will affect employment, experts said. NEW CO-WORKERS WITH NO DESKS In Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province, 29-year-old entrepreneur Zhang Qianchao has taken the idea a step further. He put together a workforce of around 80 AI agents to set up a cross-border e-commerce venture for custom baseball caps. "Agents not only assist me with design and analysis, but also help me connect efficiently with potential clients," Zhang said. New to cross-border e-commerce, he used AI tools to build a workflow spanning product selection, design and overseas delivery, doing so in just two months. Zhang's online store began receiving orders from markets including Europe and the United States less than two months after its launch. Now he can generate over 2,000 new cap designs a month. AI agents can help businesses cut costs and improve efficiency in repetitive, rule-based tasks such as customer service and marketing, said Chen Xi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Macroeconomic Research under the National Development and Reform Commission. As companies accelerate their digital transformation, however, AI agents are extending automation beyond routine processes to more complex decision-making tasks, helping the technology gain traction and opening up new market opportunities, Chen added. ADOPTION GATHERS PACE The rise of the open-source OpenClaw project earlier this year put AI agents in the public spotlight in China. Chinese technology giants have since rolled out workplace products like Doubao Work, QwenWork and Kimi Work, while businesses are increasingly adopting such tools across a growing range of operations. At dairy producer Mengniu, employee Wang Guoyin used Tencent's WorkBuddy platform to develop an AI-assisted cattle diagnostic tool, drawing on veterinary literature and his farm experience, and achieving success despite having no programming background. When farm workers report symptoms like reduced appetite, a body temperature of 39.5 degrees Celsius or falling milk production, the agent asks follow-up questions and provides diagnostic suggestions. The company said the time needed to assess a case at an individual farm had fallen from roughly 1.5 days to two hours. AI agents are finding their way into more business operations. A survey by Chinese research organization Shaqiu think tank found that the share of Chinese enterprises using AI agents had climbed from 17.3 percent at the end of 2024 to 40.3 percent in the first half of 2026. Advances in foundation models from Chinese developers including DeepSeek, Zhipu and MiniMax, alongside improvements in key capabilities such as task understanding, planning, tool use and multi-agent collaboration, have helped speed up the adoption of AI agents, said Zhong Xinlong, a researcher at the China Center for Information Industry Development. THE BROADER TEST Yet wider adoption does not necessarily translate into financial returns for businesses. KPMG's global tech report 2026 found that 88 percent of surveyed organizations were incorporating agentic AI into their systems, but only 24 percent reported achieving a return on investment across multiple AI use cases. One challenge is that AI agents still lack the reliability needed to perform lengthy tasks over extended periods, limiting their adoption in core business operations. As a result, companies have yet to see widespread returns on their investments, Zhong said. Security is another constraint on wider adoption. Risks such as data leaks, unauthorized operations and loss of control over agents' behavior continue to hinder their large-scale deployment, Zhong added. Beyond the business scenario, the spread of AI agents is also raising questions about the future of work. Against this backdrop, China is seeking to balance efforts to expand AI applications with measures to cushion their impact on employment. Under its "AI plus" initiative, China aims to raise the adoption rate of applications, including AI agents and next-generation smart terminals, to more than 90 percent by 2030. At the same time, guidelines issued last month call for using AI to both create jobs and improve employment opportunities while mitigating job displacement. The transition could bring mismatches in the labor market, with routine jobs coming under pressure even while demand for workers with interdisciplinary skills remains unmet, said Lyu Weifeng, secretary-general of the China Software Industry Association. "People are the ultimate purpose of technological development. In the age of AI and automation, it is even more important to put people first and recognize human value," noted Lu Ming, a professor of economics at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, located in east China. ■

item.title: Chinese giant panda Ran Ran jets off to Belgium
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-28
This photo taken on Nov. 28, 2026 shows the cage loaded with giant panda Ran Ran inside an airplane at the Chengdu Tianfu International Airport in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province. (Xinhua) CHENGDU, Nov. 28 (Xinhua) -- Ran Ran, a 9-year-old female giant panda, departed from southwest China's Sichuan Province on Saturday bound for Belgium, where she will stay at the Pairi Daiza zoo, as part of an ongoing conservation and research program involving the two countries. Born on May 31, 2017, Ran Ran has a round face, a well-proportioned figure, a gentle temperament, and strong adaptability to new surroundings, according to the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda (CCRCGP). She will replace Hao Hao, a female panda who has already returned to China from Belgium due to health problems. Hao Hao was sent to Belgium together with Xing Hui in 2014 to begin a 15-year cooperative conservation program. During her stay at Pairi Daiza, Hao Hao gave birth to three panda cubs who have returned to China on schedule under the cooperation agreement. Ran Ran was accompanied on the flight by a Chinese veterinarian and a Belgian keeper. Her supplies included fresh bamboo, bamboo shoots, specially prepared steamed corn buns, fruits and medications. Ran Ran also underwent a health checkup and adaptability training prior to departure. The Chinese veterinarian will remain in Belgium for a while to help the bear adapt to its new environment, the CCRCGP said. The Belgian zoo has also made extensive preparations for Ran Ran's arrival, such as upgrading its enclosure, securing a sufficient supply of the required food, and assembling an experienced animal care team. Notably, 2026 marks the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Belgium. Ran Ran's trip to Belgium will further promote in-depth cooperation between the two countries in fields like rare wildlife conservation, public education, and the sharing of scientific research and technology. According to a supplementary agreement signed in September between the China Wildlife Conservation Association and Pairi Daiza, Ran Ran will not participate in breeding during her stay in Belgium. ■ Staff members see off giant panda Ran Ran at the Wolong Shenshuping base of the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda in southwest China's Sichuan Province on Nov. 27, 2026. (Xinhua) This photo taken on Nov. 27, 2026 shows giant panda Ran Ran at the Wolong Shenshuping base of the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda in southwest China's Sichuan Province. (Xinhua) Giant panda Ran Ran looks out from the cage at the Chengdu Tianfu International Airport in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province on Nov. 28, 2026. (Xinhua)

item.title: Nagasaki A-bomb museum begins replacing "Nanjing Massacre" with "Nanjing Incident"
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-28
TOKYO, Nov. 28 (Xinhua) -- The city of Nagasaki in southwestern Japan has unveiled updated exhibition materials for its Atomic Bomb Museum, in which references to the Nanjing Massacre are replaced with the term "Nanjing Incident," Kyodo News reported. The materials were presented Friday at a meeting of the museum's operation council. City officials claimed at the meeting that the change was based on descriptions in mainstream Japanese history textbooks and official terminology used by Japan's Foreign Ministry. Several council members expressed concern, warning that the revised wording could draw international criticism. Some of the exhibition updates have already begun, with the entire process expected to be completed by mid-March 2027. The proposed change had already drawn opposition from various quarters when it was first disclosed. Takakage Fujita, secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, pointed out that the museum's operation council had been infiltrated by right-wing forces. He noted that the Nanjing Massacre was one of the most brutal crimes committed by Japan in its modern history and stands as an emblematic event demonstrating the nature of Japan's war of aggression. Eighty-one years after the end of the war, Nagasaki is taking advantage of the museum's exhibit renewal to replace the historical description of "massacre" with the term "Nanjing Incident," which denies the aggressive nature of the brutal act, Fujita said, adding that such a move is unacceptable under any circumstances. ■

item.title: China makes record discovery with complete southern mammoth skull fossil
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-28
XINING, Nov. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese researchers have discovered the country's first complete fossilized skull of a southern mammoth in the Gonghe Basin, located on the northeastern edge of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. The skull, measuring 75 centimeters long and 70 centimeters wide and paired with a set of tusks, was unearthed in August by a team from the Qinghai provincial geological survey institute. Researchers spotted a 15-centimeter bone fragment at a cliff while tracing paleontological clues in the Gonghe Basin. Subsequent identification by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology under the Chinese Academy of Sciences confirmed the specimen as a southern mammoth dating back approximately 2 million to 1.3 million years. Remarkably well-preserved and highly complete, the fossil represents a departure from previously found fragmented pieces, offering crucial evidence for understanding the migration and evolution of mammoths across the Eurasian continent. This newly discovered specimen is expected to enable the first direct comparison between East Asian and Western European skull specimens from the same evolutionary stage, noted Pan Tong, chief scientist at the Bureau of Geology and Mineral Exploration and Development of Qinghai Province. It adds a crucial link to the physical evidence chain needed to verify the west-to-east migration route of southern mammoths and to reconstruct the timeline of their spread to the northeastern end of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, according to Pan. Zhang Hailong, head of the research team, said the team will conduct meticulous specimen restoration, 3D scanning, and multidisciplinary testing to deepen research into the paleoecological evolution of the plateau. ■

item.title: China's logistics sector maintains steady growth with demand upgrades
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-28
BEIJING, Nov. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's logistics sector maintained steady growth in the first 10 months of 2026, with demand increasingly driven by emerging and high-end industries, official data showed Saturday. The total value of national social logistics reached 312.4 trillion yuan (about 46.6 trillion U.S. dollars) from January to October, up 4.8 percent year on year, according to data from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. Industrial logistics demand showed a shift toward higher-end manufacturing. From January to October, the value of industrial goods logistics rose 5.3 percent year on year. In October alone, logistics demand from high-tech manufacturing grew 17.6 percent year on year, marking its fastest monthly expansion in nearly five years. "The growth in logistics demand is increasingly concentrated in equipment manufacturing and high-tech manufacturing, reflecting upgrades in the structure used to transport goods," said Liu Yuhang, chief engineer of the federation. On the import side, while the total value of import goods logistics declined 0.6 percent year on year in the first 10 months, that of imports of mechanical and electrical products and high-tech products rose 35 percent and 44.4 percent, respectively. In the January-October period, China's logistics industry generated 12.3 trillion yuan in revenue, up 4.2 percent year on year. Revenue at major logistics enterprises grew 6.5 percent, while their operating costs per 100 yuan of revenue fell to 94.5 yuan, down 0.5 yuan from the first three quarters. Looking ahead, Liu said logistics demand is expected to receive a seasonal boost toward the end of the year, driven by e-commerce promotions and increased year-end production activities. With policy measures to develop the logistics networks taking effect and digital and green transformation gathering pace, China's logistics sector is expected to maintain steady growth while further improving quality and efficiency throughout the year, providing strong support for the recovery of the real economy, Liu said. The logistics networks are one of the six networks prioritized during China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), alongside water networks, new-type power grids, computing power networks, next-generation communication networks and urban underground pipeline networks. In a plan to develop the logistics networks unveiled earlier this year, China set goals to advance the development of the country's logistics network, including bringing total social logistics costs to 13.1 percent of GDP by 2030, down 0.8 percentage points from the end of 2025. ■

item.title: Shenzhou-23, Shenzhou-24 astronauts complete in-orbit handover
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-28
JIUQUAN, Nov. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Shenzhou-23 and Shenzhou-24 astronauts held an in-orbit handover ceremony in China's Tiangong space station on Saturday, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreign national entering Tiangong, will return to Earth with the Shenzhou-23 astronauts Zhang Zhiyuan and Li Jiaying, the agency said. Shenzhou-23 astronaut Zhu Yangzhu, who has already spent six months in orbit for a year-long stay experiment, will remain aboard the space station for the Shenzhou-24 mission together with commander Tang Hongbo and astronaut Wu Yi. The returning astronauts have finished all their scheduled tasks. They are expected to return to the Dongfeng landing site in north China aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft in the coming days, and Zhang will serve as commander of the return mission, the CMSA said. They will bring back Earth "mysterious gifts" from Tiangong, the agency added. At present, the landing site and all systems involved are busy putting the final touches on preparations to welcome the astronauts home. ■

item.title: Beyond the gibbons, China's tropical rainforest regains its rhythm
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-28
* The Hainan gibbon population has rebounded from fewer than 10 to 44. * Conservation efforts are restoring Hainan's rainforest ecosystem and benefiting local communities. * Hainan's experience offers lessons for global biodiversity conservation. HAIKOU, Nov. 28 (Xinhua) -- At 4:30 a.m., long before daylight touched Bawangling, a mountainous area of Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park in south China, Li Wenyong and his fellow wildlife monitors set out with flashlights, threading their way along narrow forest trails. They moved as quietly as possible, knowing that a single unexpected sound could frighten away the Hainan gibbons they had come to track. As dawn broke, the forest came alive with the gibbons' calls. Low, short hoots rose into long, piercing whoops that echoed through the valleys. "Everyone loves the gibbons' songs," Li said. "Protecting the gibbons means protecting the entire rainforest." For decades, those distinctive calls were at risk of disappearing. More than 40 years ago, fewer than 10 Hainan gibbons remained. Today, the population has rebounded to 44 individuals in seven family groups, a turnaround that reflects decades of efforts to protect both these animals and their habitat. Among the world's 20 surviving gibbon species, the Hainan gibbon is the only one with a population that has shown sustained growth, according to local conservation authorities. Hainan Province is home to China's largest, best-preserved and most concentrated stretch of contiguous island tropical rainforest. This forest plays a vital role in conserving water, storing carbon, supporting biodiversity and sustaining local livelihoods. In October 2021, China established Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park, bringing more than 20 previously separate nature reserves and forest parks under unified management. Covering over 4,269 square kilometers, the park hosts 4,367 recorded species of higher plants and 651 vertebrate species. It is one of China's first five national parks, which together protect some of the country's most important ecosystems, including giant panda habitats in Sichuan, Gansu and Shaanxi provinces and tiger and leopard habitats in northeast China. China has also implemented its national park law and revised regulations on nature reserves, marking a new stage of law-based and standardized development for its nature reserve system with national parks as the main body. In Hainan, conservation efforts have focused on restoring habitats, creating ecological corridors to connect fragmented forest areas, strengthening wildlife monitoring, and involving local communities in conservation. "The rainforest ecosystem is gradually finding its natural rhythm again," said Chen Kang, director of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park Administration. More than 90 new species have been discovered in Hainan's tropical rainforest in recent years, noted Zhou Runbang, an official with the provincial forestry department. Fan Pengfei, a professor at Sun Yat-sen University, said efforts to protect flagship species and their habitats have helped restore the wider ecosystem, taking conservation in Hainan beyond individual species to the forest as a whole. The benefits of rainforest conservation, notably, extend beyond wildlife to local communities. Over the past five years, the national park in Hainan has recruited 1,593 local residents as full-time ecological rangers, while ecological compensation has benefited 372 village collectives and 6,194 rural households. The park's gross ecosystem product (GEP), a measure of the economic value of ecosystem services, reached 208.97 billion yuan (around 31.15 billion U.S. dollars) in 2024, according to a think-tank report. Ecotourism is growing, supported by a 466-kilometer scenic highway linking attractions and villages of the Li and Miao ethnic groups across nine cities and counties in Hainan. Hainan is also seeking UNESCO World Heritage status for its tropical rainforest and the traditional settlement of the Li ethnic group, which have been jointly added to the World Heritage tentative list. Speaking at the 2026 Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem Partners Conference recently held in Haikou, capital of Hainan, Carlos Aldeco, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations representative in China, described Hainan as an example of how nature conservation and sustainable development can go hand in hand. He highlighted the province's efforts to protect biodiversity while creating opportunities for environmental education, sustainable livelihoods and responsible ecotourism. As climate change intensifies and extreme weather events become more frequent, tropical rainforests face growing risks of habitat degradation and biodiversity loss. Paul Shrivastava, co-president of the Club of Rome, said China's concept of ecological civilization encourages people to live sustainably within ecosystems rather than simply extracting resources from nature. Shrivastava commended China for being at the forefront of such efforts, saying its actions could help drive positive change around the world. But protecting tropical rainforests also requires cooperation across borders. Zhang Xinsheng, former president of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), said no country or organization can protect tropical rainforests in isolation, calling for closer collaboration across countries, sectors and scientific disciplines to share knowledge and address common threats. The IUCN has introduced this experience to the international community as an example of "Chinese wisdom, Hainan experience and the Bawangling Model." Hainan has also led the establishment of the Global Gibbon Network, with its secretariat located at the Hainan Institute of National Park, bringing together 36 conservation institutions from 11 countries to jointly carry out gibbon conservation research. Back in Bawangling, the results of conservation are visible in the footage collected by Li and his fellow wildlife monitors. Their videos now regularly show gibbons swinging along ropes installed to help them cross gaps in the forest canopy, while each morning, their calls continue to echo through the valleys. "I hope I can keep hearing them forever," Li said.■ (Video reporters: Guo Liangchuan and Wu Maohui; video editors: Wu You and Li Qin.)
